title: Introduction
lesson: A design begins with a promise to someone using the system. Trace one action from input to outcome, then identify what could make that promise expensive or impossible to keep.
example: A note app can save edits on the phone instantly. Sharing those edits with a collaborator requires a second promise about when they arrive.
question: A team hopes to support shared notes. Which question most directly shapes its design?
answers: How quickly must an edit appear on the other person's screen?
What will the database tables be named?
Which JSON property should hold the title?
why: The allowed delay determines whether occasional background sync is enough or whether collaborators need a live connection.
detail: Sketch a small piece of the product first. For a note app, follow a single note through create, close and reopen. Which component can still produce the note if the phone loses power? Now add a second phone. Naming the new decision about conflicting edits is already a useful design outcome, even before choosing a database.

terms.definition: An action the product must support, such as retrieving a saved note.
A limit the solution must work within, such as an offline device or a fixed storage budget.

references.title: System Design: Complete Guide with Patterns, Examples, and Techniques
A comprehensive guide to system design

story.intro: Mina writes her grocery list on a train. She closes the app as the train enters a tunnel. Will the list be there when she reopens it?
story.meaning: Start designing by naming one action someone takes and what they should be able to rely on afterward.

steps.label: types
steps.caption: The screen shows “rice,” but text on a screen can disappear when the app closes.

steps.label: saves locally
steps.caption: If the promise is “open it again offline,” the phone needs a lasting copy.

steps.label: loads from
steps.caption: Reading that copy fulfills the promise even while the train has no signal.

story.technology: A browser app can use IndexedDB, storage kept on the device, to reopen a locally saved list.

title: What is System Design?
lesson: System design connects user requirements to components, data flows and operating constraints. A useful design explains who owns each piece of data and how the system behaves under load or failure.
example: For a ticket sale, the booking service owns reservations. Search can show slightly old seat counts because the final reservation checks the authoritative record.
question: Which decision most directly prevents two buyers from booking the same seat?
answers: Choose where and how a seat reservation commits atomically.
Refresh the search results twice as often.
Add another copy of the seat map to each client.
why: A single authoritative reservation decision lets the system enforce the one-buyer rule even when clients see old seat maps.
detail: Draw a box only when you can explain which decision or data it owns. Then annotate the arrows with what crosses them and what counts as success. If a payment service sends a receipt, ask whether the charge must already be durably recorded. That answer changes the operation ordering and recovery plan.

terms.definition: The accepted input, expected result and failure behavior that components agree on.
A rule that must remain true after every allowed operation, such as one reservation per seat.

references.title: System Design: Complete Guide with Patterns, Examples, and Techniques
A comprehensive guide to system design

story.intro: Two friends tap “book” on the last seat at a pottery class. What should happen on their screens?
story.meaning: System design decides which parts of a product do which jobs, how they exchange information and who gets the final say when requests collide.

steps.label: request
steps.caption: Each phone saw the same free seat before either friend tapped.

steps.label: tries to reserve
steps.caption: The service asks storage to claim seat 8 only if it is still free. One request wins.

steps.label: replies separately
steps.caption: One friend receives a booking number. The other can pick a different class.

story.technology: A SQL database can enforce a unique booking for each class and seat even when two web servers handle the requests.

title: How to approach System Design?
lesson: Clarify the user's actions and the guarantees each needs. Estimate peak load and data size, sketch the simplest working path, then test it against a bottleneck or outage.
example: For a photo feed, estimate uploads separately from views. A million daily readers say little about peak upload bandwidth.
question: A feed must serve a million users. What information should you seek before choosing its storage layout?
answers: Peak read and write rates, object sizes and access patterns.
The exact number of replicas a competitor runs.
The longest possible name for a feed item.
why: How clients read and write data determines which operations must stay cheap and how much capacity they need.
detail: Put units on every estimate. Ten uploads per second at two megabytes each means twenty megabytes per second arriving before duplication or compression. Next, decide whether that is a typical or a peak rate. A diagram that survives an ordinary weekday may need a different bottleneck analysis for the minute concert tickets go on sale.

terms.definition: The highest demand expected during a specified interval.
A rough calculation with stated assumptions that tests whether a design is in the right range.

references.title: Intro to Architecture and Systems Design Interviews

story.intro: A school wants a photo wall for sports day. Before drawing servers, find out what will happen at the finish line.
story.meaning: Start with a user's action, estimate the busiest moment, sketch its path, then test the sketch against one likely problem.

steps.label: describes rush
steps.caption: The class expects 10 photos each second just after a race finishes.

steps.label: at 2 MB each
steps.caption: The upload path must accept about 20 megabytes every second during that rush.

steps.label: tested against
steps.caption: Try that rate and check where photos wait. The slowest part tells you what needs changing.

story.technology: A load test can send sample photos to an upload endpoint at the estimated peak rate and time completed uploads.

title: Performance vs Scalability
lesson: Performance describes what a system achieves at a given load and resource budget. Scalability describes how well it handles more work as resources increase.
example: A faster query cuts response time on one server. Adding a second server doubles capacity only if the workload can be shared and the database keeps up.
question: Which observation shows that an API scales across servers?
answers: Doubling servers nearly doubles sustainable requests per second at the same latency target.
One request finishes faster after a query rewrite.
A faster processor lowers median response time at the original traffic level.
why: Holding the latency target fixed reveals whether extra resources actually support more concurrent work.
detail: Benchmark different loads using the same mix of reads and writes. Record completed requests, errors and latency as you add servers. A shared lock can make a single worker fast yet leave eight workers waiting their turn. If their wait time dominates, reducing the time spent inside the lock can help more than adding more workers.

terms.definition: Competition among operations for a resource that can serve only limited work at once.
The resource or step currently limiting the rate at which the whole workload can finish.

story.intro: Your search page feels snappy at home. Will it still feel snappy when the whole class searches together?
story.meaning: Performance describes how a system behaves at one workload. Scalability describes how much extra work it can handle when you give it more resources.

steps.label: serves
steps.caption: At this load almost every search finishes within your 200-millisecond target.

steps.label: tested at
steps.caption: Almost every search still meets the same target. Added capacity handles nearly twice the work.

steps.label: tested at
steps.caption: Requests start queuing at the shared database. Adding web servers alone has a limit.

story.technology: A load test can record completed requests per second alongside the percentage finishing within 200 milliseconds.

title: Latency vs Throughput
lesson: Latency is the elapsed time for one operation. Throughput counts completed operations per unit of time. Batching can improve throughput while an individual item waits longer.
example: A mail worker sends 100 messages in one network call. Waiting to fill the batch delays the first message even if the worker sends more messages per second.
question: A batcher sends more emails per minute but recipients wait longer. Which change did you observe?
answers: Higher throughput and higher latency.
Higher throughput and lower latency.
Lower throughput and higher latency.
why: Completions per minute rose while elapsed time per email also rose. The two measurements track different experiences.
detail: A dashboard can report a healthy average while a small group waits several seconds. Track a high percentile alongside completion rate. If requests arrive steadily at 110 per second and workers sustain only 100, the waiting line grows by about ten each second. Latency can keep rising even while the completion graph stays flat.

terms.definition: The time at or below which roughly 99% of measured requests finish.
Time spent waiting for a resource before processing begins.

story.intro: A photo printer groups orders into batches. More prints leave the shop each minute, yet your own print takes longer.
story.meaning: Latency is the time one item takes from start to finish. Throughput is how many items finish in a period.

steps.label: prints
steps.caption: In this example a photo with an idle printer finishes in one second.

steps.label: prints in
steps.caption: Sending ten together saves setup work. With full batches the printer can finish 120 per minute.

steps.label: waits for
steps.caption: If it waits four seconds to fill the batch, its print takes nine seconds from arrival to completion.

story.technology: A worker can record a job's arrival and completion times and count all completed jobs per minute.

title: Availability vs Consistency
lesson: When replicas lose contact, a request may reach a node missing the newest write. Some operations can safely return local data. Others must wait or fail until the system can establish a single current value.
example: A cafe directory can show yesterday's opening hours during a partition. Selling the last concert seat requires stronger coordination.
question: Two disconnected regions both think seat 12 is free. Which choice preserves a single confirmed reservation?
answers: Require an authoritative decision before confirming the seat.
Confirm locally in both regions and merge the bookings later.
Shorten the time each region caches the seating chart.
why: Local confirmation can promise the seat twice. Coordination may make booking unavailable in one region but preserves the reservation rule.
detail: Write down the promise separately for browsing, booking and confirmation. During a connection failure a shop could display a cached product page while turning off the final stock commitment. For another policy, it could issue each region a limited inventory allocation in advance. Then a region can sell locally until its allocation runs out without overselling the total.

terms.definition: A communication failure that prevents some parts of a distributed system from exchanging needed messages.
A read from a copy that has not incorporated a newer write.

story.intro: Two kiosk screens show the last picnic table. The link between kiosks breaks just before two families tap reserve.
story.meaning: A kiosk could confirm a booking from its own copy, even while the other kiosk is offline. But if both confirm the last table, one family will lose it. A booking system may make someone wait so it can keep that promise.

steps.label: loses contact
steps.caption: Each still has an earlier record saying the table is free.

steps.label: can display
steps.caption: A slightly old map is still useful to visitors browsing the park.

steps.label: pauses
steps.caption: Only the north site can confirm a reservation in this design. The south kiosk cannot safely promise the table.

story.technology: A booking API can return cached park information while requiring a reachable reservation database before issuing a confirmation.

title: CAP Theorem
lesson: CAP concerns a network partition that prevents replicas from exchanging messages. During that partition a distributed register cannot guarantee both linearizable reads and writes and a successful response to every request at a functioning node.
example: After a write in Sydney, an isolated Tokyo replica receives a read. Without new information it must risk a stale answer or withhold a successful response.
question: A replica cannot reach the side that just accepted a write. What conflict does CAP expose?
answers: It may have to refuse a read to guarantee the latest value.
It must discard all previously stored data.
It can preserve both guarantees by waiting without a time limit for every partition.
why: A partition can last indefinitely. Waiting forever fails the availability requirement, while returning a local value risks violating linearizability.
detail: Imagine two histories visible to a disconnected replica. In the first, a remote writer changed a flag to green. In the second, no writer did. The replica receives exactly the same messages in both histories, so it cannot distinguish them. Any immediate answer can be wrong in one history. Adding faster CPUs does nothing to supply the missing information.

terms.definition: A value clients can read and replace, used as a small model for reasoning about a storage system.
The guarantee that operations behave as if they occurred in a single order consistent with real time.

story.intro: A lamp switch in one building changes from off to on. A screen in another building loses its network link at that exact moment.
story.meaning: CAP stands for consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. A partition is a break in communication. While the link is broken, the east screen has a choice. It can answer now and risk showing an old value, or wait to check what the west side saved.

steps.label: saves
steps.caption: The west system confirms the change before anyone asks the east screen.

steps.label: blocks update
steps.caption: From the east side, the history looks identical to one in which nobody touched the switch.

steps.label: must decide
steps.caption: Answering “off” can be stale. Waiting for a link that never recovers would leave the request unanswered.

story.technology: You can demonstrate CAP with two value stores by pausing messages between them, writing to one and then reading from the other.

title: AP - Availability + Partition Tolerance
lesson: An AP design keeps accepting operations at reachable replicas during a partition, even if their views diverge. The application needs rules for reconciling updates after communication resumes.
example: Two offline editors can add different shopping-list items. A merge can keep both additions, but simultaneous deletion and editing need an explicit rule.
question: A shared list accepts edits on both sides of a network split. Which design decision remains essential?
answers: Specify how divergent edits merge after reconnection.
Require each edit to lock both sides first.
Treat each local view as globally current.
why: Independent writes can conflict. A merge policy gives those conflicts predictable meaning for the user.
detail: Picking a winner by timestamp gives replicas a simple rule for resolving two writes, but it can erase an edit. A counter can use a different representation. If each region keeps its own monotonic contribution and replicas merge each contribution by its maximum, independent increments survive retries and later reconciliation. The choices depend on what the data means.

terms.definition: The rule for combining or choosing among changes accepted without coordination.
A counter whose value only increases, which makes older and newer copies easier to compare.

story.intro: You add tea to a shared list on a flight. Your flatmate adds bread from home before your phone reconnects.
story.meaning: An availability-first design accepts changes on reachable copies during a network split and defines how those changes will be combined later.

steps.label: adds
steps.caption: The phone saves a local addition and tells you it succeeded while offline.

steps.label: adds
steps.caption: Your flatmate gets a successful response without waiting for your phone.

steps.label: merge additions
steps.caption: Each addition carries its own identity, so both copies can keep both items after exchanging changes.

story.technology: An offline list app can store additions under distinct IDs in IndexedDB and merge matching IDs when devices synchronize.

title: CP - Consistency + Partition Tolerance
lesson: A CP design preserves a single observable order for operations through a partition. A replica that cannot establish authority can reject or delay an operation.
example: With three voting replicas, a majority can elect a leader. A lone isolated replica cannot safely declare itself leader just because its peers are silent.
question: A three-voter consensus group splits two against one. Which side can usually commit a new entry after election?
answers: The connected pair with a majority.
The isolated voter if its local clock is newer.
Both sides if clients use different endpoints.
why: A majority intersects every other majority. The isolated node cannot collect enough votes to commit a conflicting history.
detail: For five voters, a majority requires three. Only a group that can collect enough votes can elect and maintain a leader able to commit new entries. In a three-versus-two split, the smaller group may still answer liveness checks. Allowing its clients to treat tentative local writes as committed would break the promise of a single history.

terms.definition: A set of participants large enough to make a decision under a protocol's rules.
A protocol by which participants agree on decisions despite specified failures.

story.intro: Three servers keep the official count of remaining concert seats. One loses contact with the other two.
story.meaning: A consistency-first design lets only servers with enough agreement confirm changes during a split. A customer reaching an isolated server may need to try again.

steps.label: split into
steps.caption: The pair can still exchange votes. The third server cannot tell whether its peers are down or merely unreachable.

steps.label: commits
steps.caption: Two votes form a majority of three and can confirm the next change under the voting protocol.

steps.label: withholds
steps.caption: Its old seat count cannot establish who owns a remaining seat. It must avoid confirming a competing reservation.

story.technology: An etcd cluster uses the Raft voting protocol and needs a majority of members to commit new writes.

title: Consistency Patterns
lesson: A consistency model states what clients may observe when operations overlap or replicas lag. Specify the promise per workflow, such as reading your own edits, seeing updates in order, or seeing the latest completed write.
example: A profile service can route a user's next read to the writer. This gives immediate feedback while other viewers continue using lagging read replicas.
question: An author must see their new bio immediately, but other viewers can wait. Which guarantee directly fits?
answers: Read-your-writes for the author.
A single global order for all profile operations.
Eventual convergence alone with arbitrary replica reads.
why: Read-your-writes ties the author's later read to their earlier write. Other clients can still use eventually updated copies.
detail: Ask what sequence a single person can see. Someone might read a document at revision 12 and then reach a lagging server that shows revision 10. A client can carry the highest revision it has seen. A server can wait until it reaches that revision or route the read elsewhere, adding delay when replicas are far apart.

terms.definition: A session guarantee that later reads do not go backward to an earlier version.
A promise about observations made within one client's sequence of operations.

story.intro: Ari changes their profile picture and refreshes. One screen still shows the old photo, while another already shows the new one.
story.meaning: A consistency pattern states what a reader is allowed to see when copies of information change at different times.

steps.label: creates
steps.caption: The editing service gives Ari a marker for the version it just saved.

steps.label: asks for
steps.caption: The app passes that marker along so Ari can see their own successful edit.

steps.label: reads
steps.caption: The product allows other viewers to see an older picture until their nearby copy catches up.

story.technology: A read API can accept a minimum-version token and use a server that has already applied that version.

title: Weak Consistency
lesson: With weak consistency, a successful write need not become visible on the next read. The term alone gives a client no bound on staleness and promises no particular convergence deadline.
example: A live game can use the most recently received position and tolerate skipped updates. A later position quickly matters more than a missing intermediate one.
question: Which use can best tolerate occasional missed updates with no immediate catch-up guarantee?
answers: Rendering intermediate cursor positions in a shared sketch.
Choosing the winner of a final-seat reservation.
Confirming a withdrawal against the latest balance.
why: A later cursor update can replace an intermediate position. The other workflows depend on a definitive decision about scarce resources.
detail: Design the receiver around what it can safely forget. A cursor can replace a previous position with the latest sequence number and discard older arrivals. That rule would lose information in an append-only conversation where every message matters. Decide whether your data describes a current state or a history of individually valuable events before tolerating gaps.

terms.definition: An ordered identifier that lets a receiver detect gaps, duplicates or older updates from a stream.
The difference between a reported state and a newer state already known elsewhere.

story.intro: You watch a teammate's cursor move across a drawing. An old position arrives after a newer one.
story.meaning: Weak consistency gives readers limited promises about which updates they will observe or how soon. For a moving pointer, seeing a useful recent position may be enough.

steps.label: sends
steps.caption: Each update contains the cursor's current position and a rising sequence number.

steps.label: receives first
steps.caption: The viewer can draw the newest known position before update 42 arrives.

steps.label: discarded by
steps.caption: Moving backward would look jumpy. The app can safely skip this intermediate point.

story.technology: A live cursor service can keep the largest sequence number seen from each participant and ignore older position packets.

title: Eventual Consistency
lesson: If updates stop and replicas can communicate and repair differences, eventually consistent replicas converge. During propagation two clients can legitimately see different values.
example: Like counts can briefly differ across regions. A reconciliation process brings them into agreement once new likes stop arriving.
question: Which outcome does eventual consistency promise under healthy communication and no further writes?
answers: Replicas ultimately agree.
Every read immediately sees the last write.
Every replica catches up within one second.
why: Convergence is the guarantee. A bound such as one second requires an additional freshness commitment.
detail: A missed update needs a route back into the system. Replicas can compare version summaries in the background, find the differing records and exchange missing changes. They also need a deterministic rule for concurrent edits. Merely broadcasting each write once leaves a disconnected replica permanently behind if nothing ever checks it again.

terms.definition: A background process through which replicas discover differences and repair them.
The outcome in which replicas that have learned the same updates agree on their state.

story.intro: Two book clubs share a reading list. One club's tablet misses a new title while its Wi-Fi is down.
story.meaning: Eventually consistent copies can show different answers for a while. If changes stop and the copies can exchange and reconcile their updates, they come to agree.

steps.label: adds
steps.caption: Its list is now A, B and C. The disconnected tablet still shows A and B.

steps.label: requests missing
steps.caption: After reconnecting, the tablet tells the server the last change it received.

steps.label: delivers
steps.caption: With the missing addition applied and no more edits, the two lists match.

story.technology: A sync service can keep a numbered change log and replay recent entries when a device reconnects.

title: Strong Consistency
lesson: For a linearizable object, each successful operation appears to take effect at one instant between its start and finish. Later reads observe completed writes in that order, while overlapping operations may legally fall in either order.
example: A newly revoked invite must fail a later redemption. Checking an arbitrarily lagging replica would weaken that promise.
question: A flag write finishes before a second client starts reading it. No other writes occur. What must a linearizable read return?
answers: The newly written value.
Either value until background sync ends.
The value previously observed by that client.
why: The two operations do not overlap. Real-time ordering therefore puts the completed write before the read.
detail: A storage service can keep a lagging follower and still give clients linearizable behavior by routing reads through a writer that verifies its current authority. Think carefully about operations on several objects. Reading two individually linearizable records in separate calls can still produce a mixed snapshot if another client changes a record between the calls.

terms.definition: An operation whose externally visible effect takes place as one indivisible step.
A view of multiple values associated with a single logical point in time.

story.intro: An organizer closes registration. A visitor who clicks the link afterward must see that registration is closed.
story.meaning: Once the app confirms that registration is closed, the next visitor should see “closed.” That promise, even if the visitor asks a different server, is one form of strong consistency. Engineers call it linearizability.

steps.label: sets
steps.caption: The app waits for the authoritative store to confirm the change.

steps.label: precedes
steps.caption: The visitor starts checking registration after the organizer sees confirmation.

steps.label: returns
steps.caption: An old server showing “open” cannot answer this lookup unless it verifies its information is current.

story.technology: An etcd client can use a linearizable read for a registration flag when callers need the latest completed value.

title: Availability Patterns
lesson: Availability improves when a healthy part of a system can keep doing useful work after a failure. Redundancy helps only when detection, traffic routing, dependencies and spare capacity also work.
example: Two API pools in separate zones survive a zone failure only if the remaining pool can handle the shifted traffic and still reach storage.
question: A service has two zones but collapses when either zone fails. What should a failover exercise test first?
answers: Whether the surviving zone can serve the entire demand and reach dependencies.
Whether both zones use the same instance names.
Whether daily average CPU looks equal across zones.
why: Normal load can hide capacity shortfalls. A realistic exercise exposes what the surviving path needs during failure.
detail: Trace a request past the web servers all the way to its data and identity checks. Two frontends that both need one unavailable token service still leave users locked out. Identify a failure that can affect several components at once, then test a degraded mode such as browsing a catalog while checkout is temporarily unavailable.

terms.definition: A set of components vulnerable to the same incident, such as a whole power zone.
Keeping selected functions available with reduced capability during a failure.

references.title: Design Patterns for High Availability: What gets you 99.999% uptime?

story.intro: One of two kitchens at a festival loses power. Can the other kitchen still serve the lunch crowd?
story.meaning: Availability patterns keep a service useful through failures. Backup capacity helps only when the surviving route and the things it depends on still work.

steps.label: loses
steps.caption: Its order terminal stops accepting lunch orders.

steps.label: routes to
steps.caption: The surviving kitchen needs its own working power supply and enough spare capacity.

steps.label: offers
steps.caption: Dropping slow dishes can keep basic service available during the outage.

story.technology: A web service can route to a second availability zone and temporarily omit a slow recommendations feature.

title: Fail-Over
lesson: Failover moves responsibility from an unhealthy component to a replacement. Detection, promotion and routing take time, and a writer failover must prevent the old writer from continuing independently.
example: A database standby promotes after losing contact with the primary. A fencing token can keep the old primary from writing if it returns.
question: A network split leaves an old primary alive after its standby promotes. What prevents two active writers?
answers: Fence the old primary before granting the new writer authority.
Declare the old host unhealthy in the dashboard.
Increase the read replica count.
why: A routing change or health label alone cannot stop a client already connected to the old primary from writing.
detail: Choose failure detection delays with care. A very short timeout can promote a standby on a busy but healthy network. A long timeout leaves clients waiting during a real outage. Measure the whole recovery interval from the user's first failed request until a representative operation succeeds, including client retries and stale route updates.

terms.definition: The target elapsed time for restoring a service after disruption.
A mechanism that prevents a former owner from continuing to modify a protected resource.

story.intro: The server recording race results freezes halfway through a meet. A second server has a copy of the scores.
story.meaning: Failover transfers a job to a replacement after a failure. For a job with one writer, the old server must lose its ability to change the official record before another takes over.

steps.label: detects
steps.caption: Missing checks start the recovery process. Silence by itself does not prove the old server is dead.

steps.label: revokes
steps.caption: Storage rejects writes carrying the previous authority token, even if the old server wakes up.

steps.label: becomes
steps.caption: The new writer receives a valid token and the scorer reconnects to it.

story.technology: A storage service can require an increasing fencing token on writes and reject any token older than the current writer's.

title: Active - Active
lesson: In active-active deployment, multiple sites handle live traffic at once. Routing and spare capacity must support a site failure. Writable data may also need coordination or conflict handling.
example: Two regions serve a catalog close to shoppers. If each normally runs at 80% capacity, either region alone cannot absorb both workloads at peak.
question: Two equal regions each run at 60% capacity. What happens if all unchanged traffic moves to one?
answers: It needs 120% of one region's capacity.
It uses 60% because both regions were active.
It uses 80% because failover halves spare capacity.
why: Each region contributes demand of 0.6 region-equivalents, so the survivor must serve 1.2 region-equivalents.
detail: Capacity planning must consider skew. If one region normally handles 70% of traffic and another handles 30%, the smaller one may need to more than triple its usual throughput during failover. Check downstream limits too. A frontend fleet with spare cores can still exhaust its database connection allowance after traffic shifts.

terms.definition: Unused capacity available to absorb a spike or another site's workload.
Selecting which location or pool receives requests, often using health and client location.

story.intro: Two regions already answer traffic for a language-learning app. What happens to the waiting line if one region drops out?
story.meaning: In active-active operation, multiple locations serve real users at the same time. The surviving location needs room for traffic that used to go elsewhere.

steps.label: handles
steps.caption: It can serve at most 100 per second in this example.

steps.label: also handles
steps.caption: Another 100-per-second region serves the other half of 120 requests each second.

steps.label: shifts load to
steps.caption: The survivor receives 120 requests each second but can finish only 100. Without relief the queue grows by 20 per second.

story.technology: A regional load test can send the combined peak traffic to one pool to check its failure capacity.

title: Active - Passive
lesson: One deployment serves the workload while another waits to take over. A warm standby reduces recovery time, but keeping it configured, funded and ready takes continuing effort.
example: A standby checkout service runs with fewer instances. Its recovery time includes scaling up and loading caches before it can handle the full sale.
question: A warm standby responds to health checks. Which test gives stronger evidence of readiness?
answers: Shift representative traffic and measure recovery and correctness.
Check that standby software versions have similar names.
Verify that the standby returns an empty homepage.
why: Handling real demand exercises promotion, capacity, configuration and dependencies together.
detail: Think through what the standby already has before promotion. A running application with a fresh data copy can recover quickly. A backup image that first needs restoring costs less to keep but lengthens the outage. Track the age of the standby's latest recoverable data separately from the time required to bring it online.

terms.definition: A partially running replacement that needs some preparation or scaling before serving all traffic.
The target maximum amount of recent data loss, measured as elapsed time before failure.

story.intro: A gallery sells tickets from one location while a second ticket service waits on standby. How long will a switch actually take?
story.meaning: One ticket service does the work while another waits to take over. The backup may need time to start enough servers or load the latest ticket data.

steps.label: copies bookings to
steps.caption: The standby has a recent booking record but serves no ordinary ticket traffic.

steps.label: triggers
steps.caption: The replacement first needs authority to issue tickets and enough capacity for visitors.

steps.label: switches to
steps.caption: A successful purchase shows that the recovery path works from a customer's perspective.

story.technology: A database failover drill can time a real test purchase and check which pre-failure bookings survived on the promoted standby.

title: Replication
lesson: Replication transfers changes among copies of data. Waiting for confirmation from other copies can improve durability at the cost of write latency or availability. Asynchronous copies can lag.
example: A primary acknowledges a new note immediately, then fails before the standby receives it. Promoting the standby can lose the acknowledged note.
question: Which risk follows from acknowledging writes before asynchronous replication finishes?
answers: A promoted replica may lack acknowledged writes.
Reads at the primary always become slower.
The primary must wait for every replica.
why: An acknowledgment can reach the client while the only copy of the new write is still on the failed primary.
detail: A follower often replays changes from an ordered log. Watch both how far behind it is and whether it is making progress. Replication also faithfully copies accidental deletes. To recover yesterday's state after a mistaken delete, keep independent backups or enough retained history for a point-in-time restore and rehearse the restore.

terms.definition: The delay or distance between changes on the writer and changes applied on a replica.
Restoring data to a selected earlier instant, often by replaying a backup and change log.

references.title: Database Replication Introduction: Types and Advantages

story.intro: A recipe app says your edit was saved. Then its storage server fails before another server receives the change.
story.meaning: Replication keeps copies of data on multiple machines. The point at which a system says “saved” determines what the user can rely on after a failure.

steps.label: stores
steps.caption: The first machine has the edit on its own storage.

steps.label: acknowledges
steps.caption: In this asynchronous design it responds before checking whether a second machine has saved the edit.

steps.label: leaves
steps.caption: The promoted copy still has yesterday's recipe. Waiting for a second durable copy before acknowledging would change this particular outcome.

story.technology: A database can ship a continuous change log to a standby and expose how far behind that standby is.

title: Master - Slave
lesson: Also called primary-replica or leader-follower replication, this topology sends writes to one leader and copies its changes to followers. Followers can share read load when their freshness is sufficient.
example: A user updates a profile through the leader and immediately reads from a lagging follower. Routing that read to the leader can prevent the old profile from reappearing.
question: A user sees an old address just after editing it. Which action can guarantee a fresh follow-up read in this topology?
answers: Read from the leader that committed the edit, with no intervening writes.
Choose a random follower for every read.
Increase the number of asynchronous followers.
why: A follower may still be replaying earlier writes. The committing leader already holds the new value.
detail: A leader can return a marker identifying the position of a committed write in its log. A later read can present that marker to a follower. If the follower has replayed far enough it can answer locally. Otherwise the service can wait or use the leader, preserving a fresh read without sending all traffic there.

terms.definition: An identifier marking progress through a change log.
Giving a former follower authority to accept new writes after the previous leader steps aside or fails.

references.title: Database Replication Introduction: Types and Advantages

story.intro: Sam changes a parcel address and sees the old address on refresh. Their read reached a different database server.
story.meaning: Also called primary-replica, this setup has one database server accept writes. Other servers copy its changes and can serve reads as the product allows.

steps.label: updates
steps.caption: The primary saves Unit 7 and confirms the edit.

steps.label: still shows
steps.caption: The copy has not applied the newest change yet.

steps.label: reads from
steps.caption: Routing this read to the server that accepted the edit shows Unit 7 immediately.

story.technology: An application using PostgreSQL can send profile updates to the primary and use a read replica for less time-sensitive lookups.

title: Master - Master
lesson: Multi-leader replication lets multiple sites accept writes and exchange them. If two sites modify the same item before replication, the system needs an ownership rule or conflict-resolution policy.
example: Two regions edit the same display name during a partition. Keeping the latest timestamp is simple but can silently discard a meaningful edit or be misled by clock skew.
question: Which workload most naturally reduces write conflicts across two writable regions?
answers: Assign each region ownership of a disjoint set of records.
Let both regions update one global mutable counter using replacement writes.
Randomly split edits to each user profile across regions.
why: Disjoint write ownership limits how often separate leaders concurrently change the same record.
detail: Consider more than collisions on the same field. Two disconnected sites could each create a different account with the same username. Merging fields later cannot make both original uniqueness promises true. Reserve unique names centrally, give sites separate namespaces, or make the initial result provisional and explain how the conflict will be resolved.

terms.definition: A rule that a value such as a username may belong to at most one record.
Writes that proceed without either writer first seeing the other's change.

references.title: Database Replication Introduction: Types and Advantages

story.intro: Two cafés can rename the same drink while their systems are disconnected. What name will the shared menu show later?
story.meaning: Also called multi-leader replication, this lets several locations accept writes and copy them to one another. Conflicting changes need an explicit rule.

steps.label: renames drink
steps.caption: The east location commits this name before it can send the change west.

steps.label: renames drink
steps.caption: The west location independently changes the same menu entry.

steps.label: finds
steps.caption: Both cafés accepted a real edit. The app can preserve both versions for a manager to resolve.

story.technology: A multi-site menu service can assign ownership of each drink to one café to reduce concurrent changes to the same record.

title: Availability in Numbers
lesson: Define a good event, the population of eligible events and a measurement window. For a request-based target, divide good requests by eligible requests. The remainder of the target is the error budget.
example: If 999,500 of one million eligible searches succeed, request availability is 99.95%. A time-based uptime target measures a different quantity.
question: One million requests are eligible and the target is 99.9% successful. How many failures fit the budget?
why: The allowed failure fraction is 0.001. Multiplying by one million yields 1,000.
detail: A server process can stay alive while every checkout returns an error. Measure an outcome close to the user, state whether slow successes count as good, and choose the interval in advance. Compare the result by region too. A high global success fraction can hide an outage affecting a small but important population.

terms.definition: A measured signal such as the fraction of eligible purchases that finish successfully.
A target value for an indicator over a specified time window.

story.intro: A music app completed 9,980 of 10,000 song-start requests this morning. Did it meet its goal?
story.meaning: Decide what counts as success, then divide the number of successes by the number of attempts. For this app, success could mean a song actually starts within two seconds.

steps.label: include
steps.caption: Define success as playback beginning within the chosen time limit.

steps.label: equals
steps.caption: Count requests using the same definition and window as the goal.

steps.label: allows
steps.caption: Twenty starts failed, so the service used twice the allowed failures in this window.

story.technology: An API counter can record all eligible starts and the subset that begin playback within the target time.

title: 99.9% Availability - three 9s
lesson: Three nines leaves 0.1% of the measurement window for unavailability. For a time-based objective over 30 full days, that is 43.2 minutes.
example: A 30-minute outage uses about 69% of a 30-day three-nines time budget. The same outage might affect a very different share of monthly requests.
question: A service with a 30-day, time-based 99.9% target is down for 40 minutes. Roughly how much budget remains?
answers: 3.2 minutes
32 minutes
0.32 minutes
why: Thirty days contain 43,200 minutes. One thousandth of that is 43.2 minutes, leaving 3.2.
detail: In a 30-day month, a time-based 99.9% target allows about 43 minutes of downtime. A request-based target works differently. If ten times the usual traffic arrives during those 43 minutes, the same outage can consume a much larger share of the failed-request allowance. Choose the denominator before converting nines into minutes.

terms.definition: The period over which eligible events or available time are counted.
The amount of bad service an objective permits over its chosen window.

story.intro: Your club promises its ticket page will be up 99.9% of a 30-day month. Is there room for a 40-minute outage?
story.meaning: Three nines leaves one thousandth of the measurement window unavailable. For a time-based target, convert the window into minutes before calculating the allowance.

steps.label: contain
steps.caption: Multiply 30 days by 24 hours and 60 minutes an hour.

steps.label: times 0.001
steps.caption: That is the full downtime allowance for this particular month.

steps.label: minus 40 minutes
steps.caption: Another four-minute outage in the same window would put the club over its target.

story.technology: A time-based uptime report can total failed intervals during the 30-day window and compare their length with 43.2 minutes.

title: 99.99% Availability - four 9s
lesson: Four nines leaves 0.01% of a time window for unavailability. That amounts to 4.32 minutes in 30 days. An extra nine shrinks the budget tenfold.
example: A five-minute manual failover can consume more than the whole 30-day four-nines budget even if it is the only outage.
question: A team moves from 99.9% to 99.99% monthly uptime. How does its allowed downtime change?
answers: It falls to one tenth of the previous budget.
It falls by half.
It falls by one minute regardless of the window.
why: The allowed fraction changes from 0.1% to 0.01%, so the same measurement window gives one tenth the downtime.
detail: At four nines, a constant 1% error rate spends a request-based error budget one hundred times faster than the sustainable rate of 0.01%, assuming steady traffic. A team tracking this can act during a brief sharp outage and also detect a smaller persistent leak using a longer observation window.

terms.definition: How quickly an error budget is being consumed relative to the rate the objective allows.
An interval ending at the present time that advances as new measurements arrive.

story.intro: A payment team promises four nines of uptime. One five-minute interruption might sound tiny over an entire month.
story.meaning: Four nines leaves one ten-thousandth of the measured time for outages. A small change in the percentage gives you far less recovery time.

steps.label: contain
steps.caption: Use a full 30-day interval to make the comparison precise.

steps.label: times 0.0001
steps.caption: Four nines leaves about four minutes and nineteen seconds for the whole window.

steps.label: exceeds allowance by
steps.caption: The interruption alone is about 41 seconds over budget, even if everything else ran perfectly.

story.technology: A payment uptime dashboard can show remaining seconds alongside the percentage so operators can see the cost of a slow recovery.

title: Availability in Parallel vs Sequence
lesson: For independent required dependencies in sequence, multiply their availabilities. When any one of several independent replicas can serve, multiply their failure probabilities and subtract from one. Shared failures weaken this model.
example: Two independent 99% nodes in series yield 98.01%. If either can handle the full request with perfect failover, parallel availability is 99.99%.
question: Two redundant nodes share one power supply. Why might the independent parallel formula overestimate uptime?
answers: One power failure can disable both nodes together.
Parallel service always requires every node to be healthy.
The calculation should add the two uptime percentages.
why: The formula assumes independent failures and successful routing. A shared power supply makes some failures correlated.
detail: Write a success condition before multiplying probabilities. A page might require login and inventory, yet tolerate a broken recommendations widget. Including that widget as required would understate availability. Conversely, assuming two storage replicas are independent overlooks software bugs deployed to both. Draw the dependency structure for the exact user action being measured.

terms.definition: A component whose failure prevents this operation from succeeding.
One underlying cause that disables multiple components together.

references.title: System Design Primer: availability in parallel vs sequence

story.intro: A bike locker needs a working lock and a working reader. Would a second reader help if the lock still jams?
story.meaning: Required parts in sequence must all work. Interchangeable parts in parallel need only one working path. Simple probability calculations assume the failures are independent.

steps.label: requires
steps.caption: With independent failures, success is 0.99 × 0.99, or 98.01%.

steps.label: both fail
steps.caption: If either reader can open the lock, both must fail to lose the reader function. Multiply 0.01 by 0.01.

steps.label: requires
steps.caption: With perfect switching and independent failures, the whole locker reaches about 98.99%. The single lock still matters.

story.technology: A dependency diagram for a checkout flow can distinguish mandatory steps from redundant servers that can each perform the same step.

title: Background Jobs
lesson: A background job moves slow work out of the interactive request. Persist the task before acknowledging it, then use workers to process it with a retry policy and visible status.
example: A photo upload returns a receipt after saving a thumbnail job. The photo may briefly show a placeholder while the worker runs.
question: An API promises to convert a file after returning a receipt. What should happen before the receipt is sent?
answers: Durably record the work and its identifier.
Begin conversion only in a request-local variable.
Mark conversion complete so the client stops polling.
why: Once a client has a receipt, the task must survive the request handler disappearing.
detail: A worker can finish the requested work and crash before acknowledging its message. The queue may then give the same task to another worker. Make the task safe to repeat and acknowledge it after committing its output. For repeated failures, record the reason and isolate the task so one malformed input cannot block healthy jobs.

terms.definition: A signal to the queue that processing has finished and the message can be removed.
A holding area for messages that repeatedly fail processing and need inspection.

story.intro: A teacher asks a school app to export a year of photos. The export takes too long to keep the page waiting.
story.meaning: A background job records work now and lets a separate process do it later. The request can finish once the system can keep its promise to do the work.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: The app creates job 27 and saves it in a durable queue, a waiting list that survives a restart.

steps.label: returns
steps.caption: The teacher can leave the page while the export waits for a worker.

steps.label: completes
steps.caption: The worker stores the file and marks the job ready. A repeated attempt uses the same job ID.

story.technology: An export worker can read jobs from a database table and write each completed file under its job ID.

title: Event-Driven
lesson: An event records something that happened. Producers publish it so consumers can react independently, which decouples releases but requires handling duplicates, delay and sometimes reordered delivery.
example: A photo-uploaded event starts thumbnail generation. A worker writes output under a stable photo key so repeated delivery converges on the same result.
question: A worker receives the same upload event twice. What helps it avoid creating duplicate thumbnails?
answers: Use a stable event or photo identifier to make processing idempotent.
Assume each delivery represents a different upload.
Run two independent queues for the same worker.
why: A stable key lets the consumer recognize or safely repeat an already processed event.
detail: A checkout that commits an order and then publishes an event has a gap. It might crash after the commit, before publication. Recording an outgoing event in the same transaction as the order closes that gap. A separate relay publishes the record later. The relay can still publish twice, so subscribers should handle duplicate events.

terms.definition: A durable collection of outgoing messages written in the same transaction as their related business changes.
A consumer that receives events it has registered interest in.

story.intro: A library wants a newly returned book to appear on the shelf screen and notify the next reader. The returns desk should finish quickly.
story.meaning: An event announces a fact that already happened. Interested programs receive that fact and perform their own jobs.

steps.label: records
steps.caption: The library records the return and an outgoing event together so the announcement can survive a restart.

steps.label: delivers to
steps.caption: The shelf display updates its view when it receives the event for that book.

steps.label: also reaches
steps.caption: A separate program checks the waiting list. It tracks the event ID to avoid notifying the same reader twice.

story.technology: A returns service can save an event beside the return in one database transaction, then publish it from the saved record.

title: Schedule Driven
lesson: Scheduled jobs run at a time or interval. A delay, restart or overlap can make one scheduled interval execute late, twice or never, so define the time window each run owns.
example: A nightly digest uses the calendar date and account as its job key. A delayed retry can reuse that key without sending a second digest.
question: Yesterday's digest job restarts after midnight. Which input lets it finish the intended work?
answers: The original scheduled reporting window.
The current clock time each time it retries.
The most recent successful email's subject.
why: A stable interval keeps retries tied to the correct reporting period even after the date changes.
detail: Every five minutes and every day at 09:00 are different promises. Clock changes can skip or repeat a local time. Choose a time zone, define what happens after downtime, and decide whether overlapping runs can safely proceed. A ledger of completed reporting windows allows a restarted scheduler to identify a missing interval without guessing.

terms.definition: A later execution covering an interval missed while the scheduler was unavailable.
The rule governing what happens when a new scheduled execution meets a still-running predecessor.

story.intro: A reading app sends a weekly recap every Monday morning. A restart just after nine should not send one reader two recaps.
story.meaning: A schedule triggers work at a chosen time or interval. Each run needs a clear period to cover so delayed runs and retries can be handled correctly.

steps.label: starts
steps.caption: The scheduler passes the previous week's dates and the reader's ID to the job.

steps.label: records
steps.caption: Those two values identify one recap even if the worker runs on Tuesday.

steps.label: checks
steps.caption: The system reuses the same job identity and avoids starting a second send for the same completed recap.

story.technology: A scheduled worker can use a database uniqueness constraint on reader ID and week, and pass that key to a delivery service that supports deduplication.

title: Returning Results
lesson: Long-running work needs a way to associate an eventual result with the original request. A job ID and status endpoint support polling. Push notifications or webhooks reduce polling but require delivery and retry handling.
example: A PDF export returns HTTP 202 and a status URL. Once complete, the client retrieves its file using that URL.
question: A mobile client disconnects halfway through a large export. What lets it retrieve the result later?
answers: A durable job ID and an authorized status or result endpoint.
Keeping the original HTTP response open indefinitely.
A progress indicator held in the client screen.
why: A durable identifier outlives the connection and maps a returning client to the correct stored result.
detail: The status record should distinguish queued work, running work, final failure and completion. Save the output before exposing completion, or a client may follow a link to a file that doesn't exist yet. If each waiting client polls once a second, 10,000 waiting clients can create 10,000 status reads every second. A suggested retry delay limits that load.

terms.definition: Repeatedly asking for the current state of an operation.
An HTTP callback from a producer to a consumer when an event or result is ready.

story.intro: Nico requests a PDF report on their phone, then loses signal. On reconnecting, the app should find the same report.
story.meaning: A slow request can return a job receipt first. The client then uses that receipt to look up progress and retrieve the finished result.

steps.label: issues
steps.caption: The API responds that it accepted the request and gives Nico a status address for job 91.

steps.label: updates
steps.caption: The worker saves the finished PDF before changing the status to ready.

steps.label: reopens
steps.caption: The status endpoint checks Nico's access and returns the file link, even though the original connection ended.

story.technology: An HTTP API can return 202 Accepted with a status URL and serve the completed PDF after the user signs back in.

title: Domain Name System
lesson: DNS maps names to records such as IP addresses. A recursive resolver can cache answers until their time to live expires, reducing lookup work while delaying the visibility of changes.
example: Moving a service to a new IP can leave clients reaching the old address while their cached records remain valid. Plan an overlap during the move.
question: Why do some clients keep reaching an old server after its DNS record changes?
answers: Their resolvers still have a valid cached answer.
Every client must download the entire DNS zone before switching.
DNS always routes by the lowest measured latency.
why: Time to live controls how long ordinary cached records may be reused. Changing an authoritative record does not instantly empty resolver caches.
detail: On a cache miss the recursive resolver normally follows referrals down the naming hierarchy until it locates an authoritative server for the domain. An A record supplies an IPv4 address and an AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address. For a planned migration, lower the old TTL early enough for older cached answers to expire before changing the address.

terms.definition: A DNS server that publishes records for a zone it serves.
A service that looks up DNS answers on a client's behalf and often caches them.

references.title: Getting started with Domain Name System

story.intro: You type the school newspaper's name into a browser. How does your phone know which computer to contact?
story.meaning: The Domain Name System, or DNS, looks up records for names. A resolver does the lookup for your device and can reuse a recent answer.

steps.label: asks
steps.caption: The phone needs an address for the newspaper's hostname before it opens a connection.

steps.label: looks up
steps.caption: On a cache miss, the resolver follows the naming hierarchy to the server responsible for the name.

steps.label: returns
steps.caption: The phone uses that address to connect. The resolver may reuse the answer for the record's allowed lifetime.

story.technology: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address, and its time-to-live value tells ordinary resolvers how long to cache it.

title: Content Delivery Networks
lesson: A CDN places servers near users to deliver cacheable content. A cache hit avoids a trip to the origin. Cache keys, freshness and access rules determine which users can safely receive the same response.
example: A global class site caches identical lesson images at the edge. Personalized feedback requires a different cache policy to keep students' responses separate.
question: Which response is the safest fit for shared edge caching without user-specific keys?
answers: A public image with a content-hashed URL.
A private dashboard rendered for the signed-in user.
A response containing a one-time password reset link.
why: The image is intentionally identical for everyone. Sharing personalized responses across users could expose private data.
detail: Decide what makes two requests equivalent. A translated page needs a cache key that accounts for language if translations share a URL. Too few key dimensions can return the wrong representation. Too many, such as a unique tracking ID for every visitor, split identical content across many entries and reduce the benefit of caching.

terms.definition: The identifying inputs used to locate a cached representation.
The fraction of eligible requests served using cached content.

story.intro: Readers in several countries open the same large photo. Sending every copy from the photographer's server makes distant readers wait.
story.meaning: A content delivery network, or CDN, can keep copies on servers close to readers. Requests for the same public file can reuse those copies.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: The server checks for a usable cached copy of the photo.

steps.label: fetches from
steps.caption: On a miss it asks the original file server for the image and can store a copy under the photo URL.

steps.label: gets
steps.caption: A reader reaching the same cache can receive the photo without a new trip to the origin.

story.technology: A CDN can cache a public image at a versioned URL and leave private account pages outside its shared cache.

title: Push CDNs
lesson: With push distribution, a publisher sends assets to CDN storage ahead of requests. Pre-positioning can avoid a slow first fetch but transfers and stores files regardless of demand.
example: A game preloads a large release asset before launch. It pays distribution costs even in regions with few downloads.
question: A live event has a fixed opening video and a known release time. What makes push distribution appealing?
answers: The video can be staged before viewers arrive.
The initial viewer must populate the asset from origin.
The origin can change the video without publishing a new version.
why: Pre-positioning makes the first viewer less dependent on an origin fetch when a crowd arrives together.
detail: Make the release order explicit. Publish the new assets, verify that the CDN can serve them, and only then publish the page that references them. Giving each version a distinct asset URL lets older pages keep loading the matching file. Retain old versions long enough for those pages and client caches to age out.

terms.definition: A file given a different identifier or URL whenever its contents change.
A request to remove or mark old cached content unusable before normal expiry.

story.intro: A festival will reveal a trailer at noon. The first crowd should get the file without waiting for it to move from the studio.
story.meaning: With push distribution, the publisher supplies files to CDN storage before people request them. The release process decides what to place and when.

steps.label: uploads
steps.caption: The studio sends the finished file to CDN storage before announcing the release.

steps.label: checks
steps.caption: The team verifies the promised locations can serve this version before making the viewing link public.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: Prepared locations can serve immediately, even if one location ends up with very few viewers.

story.technology: A release script can upload versioned media to a push CDN's storage and publish the new viewing link after verifying delivery.

title: Pull CDNs
lesson: A pull CDN fetches content from its origin when an edge lacks a usable cached copy. Popular assets become local automatically, while cold or expired items incur origin latency.
example: A recipe site's long tail of images suits on-demand caching. The first request in a new region may be slower than later requests.
question: An image loads slowly for one visitor and quickly for later visitors in the same region. Which trace supports a pull-CDN explanation?
answers: An edge miss fetches the image from origin, then subsequent requests hit.
Every edge downloads every image on publication.
The origin processes every request and sends a fresh image every time.
why: A cold edge needs the initial fetch. Reuse of that stored response speeds up later requests.
detail: An origin can be overwhelmed when a popular object expires at many locations together. An edge can coalesce simultaneous misses for the same key, forwarding one fetch and sharing its result. A CDN can also send edge misses through a shared regional cache, lowering origin traffic at the cost of an extra hop on a miss.

terms.definition: Combining concurrent requests for the same missing item into one upstream request.
An intermediate cache that handles requests from multiple edge locations before they reach the origin.

story.intro: A wildlife archive has thousands of bird photos. A small town might only look up one local species.
story.meaning: With a pull CDN, a cache fetches a file from its source when it needs the file. Actual requests determine which files get stored at each location.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: The local CDN cache has no copy of the heron yet.

steps.label: pulls from
steps.caption: The first request pays the extra trip to retrieve the file and can populate the local cache.

steps.label: loads from
steps.caption: While the copy is fresh, the nearby cache handles the request and the archive avoids another transfer.

story.technology: A CDN distribution with an object-storage origin can fill a regional cache on the first request for each public image.

title: Load Balancers
lesson: A load balancer chooses a healthy backend for incoming traffic. Health checks and routing policies keep one address usable while instances come and go. The balancing layer itself also needs redundancy.
example: A checkout service removes a draining instance from rotation before stopping it. Existing requests get time to finish while new traffic goes elsewhere.
question: A backend process is alive but cannot serve checkout requests. Which signal helps a balancer route around it?
answers: A readiness check reflecting whether it can accept checkout traffic.
A count of historical orders for that server.
A check that its hostname is in DNS.
why: Readiness measures whether sending new work will succeed. Merely knowing the host exists misses application failures.
detail: Consider what happens during a deployment. Stop assigning new work to an instance, let in-flight requests finish, then remove it. If HTTP connections are reused, the draining policy also needs to handle requests arriving on existing connections. Without a deadline, one long-lived stream could keep the retiring instance alive indefinitely.

terms.definition: The group of eligible servers a load balancer can choose from.
A controlled retirement process that allows existing work to complete while limiting new work.

story.intro: Two servers can search the same library catalogue. When Maya looks up a book, who decides which server gets her search?
story.meaning: A load balancer is the front door for a group of servers. The app sends its request to one address. The load balancer picks a server that can take the work.

steps.label: Search for frogs
steps.caption: Maya searches for books about frogs. Her app knows the library’s address. It never needs the address of either server.

steps.label: First search
steps.caption: Both servers are ready. In this example the load balancer takes turns, so Maya’s search goes to Server A.

steps.label: Next search
steps.caption: Jo searches for cookbooks. This time Server B gets the work. Both readers still see the same catalogue.

story.technology: An AWS Application Load Balancer can take turns sending web requests to healthy servers. This turn-taking rule is called round robin.

title: LB vs Reverse Proxy
lesson: A reverse proxy receives requests on behalf of origin servers and forwards them. Load balancing is the function of distributing traffic among backends. One HTTP proxy can do both jobs.
example: A proxy that terminates TLS and forwards to a single app still serves as a reverse proxy. Adding a healthy upstream pool lets it balance traffic too.
question: A proxy terminates HTTPS and sends every request to one origin. Which statement fits?
answers: It is a reverse proxy and currently has no pool to distribute work across.
TLS termination requires it to balance across at least two origins.
It is a forward proxy because it maintains a connection to the origin.
why: The direction is defined by which side the proxy represents. A single origin is sufficient to proxy on behalf of the service.
detail: A reverse proxy can create a new upstream connection and attach information about the original request. The backend then observes the proxy as its immediate peer. If the app uses forwarded client addresses for auditing or limits, configure which proxy supplies that information and how it replaces incoming client-provided values.

terms.definition: The server a proxy contacts to fulfill a request.
Ending a client's encrypted connection at a component that can then access the plaintext request.

story.intro: A cinema site has one ticket server behind its public web address. Next month it will need a second ticket server.
story.meaning: A reverse proxy receives a request on behalf of a service and forwards it. Load balancing is the job of choosing among available destinations.

steps.label: contacts
steps.caption: The proxy handles the public connection for the cinema.

steps.label: forwards to
steps.caption: The proxy already performs its role with just one destination.

steps.label: chooses between
steps.caption: Once it distributes requests across the pair, the same component performs load balancing too.

story.technology: An NGINX reverse proxy can forward to one upstream server or select from a configured upstream group.

title: Load Balancing Algorithms
lesson: Round robin rotates across eligible backends. Weighted routing accounts for unequal capacity. Least-connections favors servers with fewer active connections when that count reflects current work.
example: A video relay holds connections open for very different durations. Counting active connections can avoid sending a new stream to a server already carrying many long streams.
question: For equal servers handling one similarly costly stream per connection with varied durations, which signal best reflects occupied slots?
answers: The current active connection count.
The total connections accepted since startup.
The backend's position in a fixed rotation.
why: Active connections count the occupied slots now. Historical totals and fixed turns ignore streams that are still open.
detail: An IP-based hash can repeatedly send a client to the same server and improve local cache reuse. A large office may share one public IP, however, concentrating many users on one backend. Weights can reflect different machine sizes. For expensive mixed workloads, observe queue depth or latency to check whether your balancing signal really tracks work.

terms.definition: A preference to send related requests to the same backend.
Rotating through backends while assigning more turns to those configured with larger weights.

story.intro: Two servers stream story time to classrooms. One class listens for a minute while another stays connected for an hour.
story.meaning: A balancing algorithm is the rule for picking a destination. The rule should use a signal that reflects the work each server is already doing.

steps.label: holds
steps.caption: Suppose each live stream occupies one equal-sized slot for as long as its class listens.

steps.label: holds
steps.caption: Although the two servers may have started a similar number of streams, B has more free slots now.

steps.label: chooses
steps.caption: Sending the next stream to B brings its count to three. This rule works here because each connection has a similar cost.

story.technology: NGINX supports a least-connections policy for upstream groups when active connection counts reflect server load.

title: Layer 7 Load Balancing
lesson: An application-layer balancer uses protocol details such as HTTP paths, hosts or headers to choose a backend. For HTTPS path routing, it needs access to the decrypted request.
example: One domain sends /images to a media service and /orders to checkout. Inspecting paths allows this split on the same port.
question: A service must route /video separately from /chat on the same HTTPS hostname. What capability is needed?
answers: Read the HTTP path after TLS termination.
Hash the destination TCP port alone.
Rotate raw connections without reading application data.
why: The path is an HTTP field inside the encrypted stream. A layer with access to HTTP can make a path-based choice.
detail: A layer 7 proxy can route individual HTTP requests carried over the same client connection to different backend services. This helps when one browser opens a long-lived connection and asks for many resources. It also puts request parsing, certificate handling and routing rules on the critical path, so measure their cost and failure behavior.

terms.definition: Named HTTP metadata that describes a request or response, such as its content type.
Choosing a destination using information available for an individual application request.

references.title: System Design Primer: layer 7 load balancing

story.intro: A workshop website sends video uploads and booking requests to different teams, all under one hostname.
story.meaning: A layer 7 balancer understands application information such as an HTTP request path. It can use that information to choose the service that handles a request.

steps.label: HTTPS request
steps.caption: Your browser connects to the workshop site. The gateway opens the encrypted request and reads the path, the part of the address after the site name.

steps.label: /videos/intro
steps.caption: The path starts with /videos, so the gateway sends this request to the servers that handle uploads.

steps.label: /bookings/new
steps.caption: When you reserve a seat, the path starts with /bookings. The same site address now leads to a different service.

story.technology: AWS Application Load Balancer and Azure Application Gateway both let teams write rules based on the path in a web address.

title: Layer 4 Load Balancing
lesson: A transport-layer balancer routes flows using information such as protocol, IP addresses and ports. It can forward encrypted connections without inspecting HTTP content.
example: A TLS service keeps decryption keys on the backends. A layer 4 balancer can spread new connections while leaving each encrypted stream intact.
question: Which request can a layer 4 balancer satisfy without decrypting traffic?
answers: Distribute new TCP connections across healthy endpoints.
Choose a backend using a session cookie.
Send requests with a particular HTTP path to a special pool.
why: Addresses, ports and connection state are available at the transport layer. Cookies and paths live inside application data.
detail: A flow often stays bound to one backend so packets for a connection reach consistent transport state. Thousands of application requests multiplexed on a single long-lived connection may therefore all reach one backend. Adding instances usually helps new connections first. Existing long-lived traffic may need time to redistribute as clients reconnect.

terms.definition: The source and destination addresses, source and destination ports, and transport protocol identifying a flow.
Carrying several independent logical exchanges over one underlying connection.

story.intro: Weather sensors send encrypted readings over long-lived connections. The collecting servers hold the keys needed to read them.
story.meaning: A layer 4 balancer assigns network connections using information such as addresses and ports. It can forward encrypted bytes to a server without opening the messages inside.

steps.label: opens TCP to
steps.caption: TCP establishes the connection that will carry this sensor's readings.

steps.label: assigns flow
steps.caption: It uses connection information to select a collector. The collector handles the encryption session.

steps.label: stay with
steps.caption: Messages on that established connection continue to the same collector. A new connection can go elsewhere.

story.technology: A network load balancer with a TCP listener can pass the sensor's encrypted stream through to its collector.

title: Horizontal Scaling
lesson: Horizontal scaling adds instances and spreads work across them. It works best when requests can run on any instance or the system can partition their state deliberately.
example: Three API instances can process independent searches. A shared database still limits growth if every search runs the same expensive query there.
question: Adding API replicas breaks shopping carts when users reach a different server. Which change makes requests portable?
answers: Store cart state in a shared durable store accessible to all replicas.
Keep a separate private cart in each server's memory.
Reduce the DNS TTL for API servers.
why: Each replica can load the same authoritative cart, so correctness no longer depends on which instance receives the next request.
detail: Adding instances takes time. If a new instance needs a minute to boot and fill its cache, a thirty-second burst may pass before reactive scaling helps. Keep headroom or pre-scale for predictable events. Before removing instances, drain active work and check whether the remaining pool can carry demand without immediately scaling back up.

terms.definition: Adjusting available capacity automatically in response to measured or anticipated demand.
An instance that does not require its own persistent per-client state to correctly handle the next request.

story.intro: A maths practice app gets busy just before a test. Adding a second web server should let either one answer a student's next question.
story.meaning: Horizontal scaling means adding more machines to share the work. If the next request goes to a different machine, that machine still needs a way to find the user’s data.

steps.label: saves answer on
