steps.caption: Server A records the answer in shared storage that both servers can read.

steps.label: lands on
steps.caption: The balancer can now assign work to B as well as A.

steps.label: reads
steps.caption: B resumes the same exercise from shared storage. The student's progress survives the change of server.

story.technology: A stateless web API can run in several containers backed by one durable progress store.

title: Application Layer
lesson: The application layer executes the product's rules behind an interface. It validates requests, checks permissions and coordinates data access. Keeping that responsibility explicit makes important decisions easier to test.
example: An API checks that an account owns a playlist before adding a song. The database transaction then commits the membership change.
question: Where should a playlist service enforce edit permission for every request?
answers: At a trusted server-side boundary before committing the edit.
Only in the browser's button visibility logic.
Only in a cache key attached to the playlist.
why: Clients can issue requests directly. The component authorizing the state change must check the caller's rights.
detail: Keep a business rule close to the state it protects. An API that checks inventory, waits, then separately writes a booking leaves time for a second caller to see the same item as free. The application can ask storage to reserve only if stock remains and use the result to decide whether to confirm or decline.

terms.definition: A modification that succeeds only if a stated condition still holds when the change happens.
The application's rules for valid actions and their effects, such as when to confirm an order.

references.title: Intro to architecting systems for scale

story.intro: Lena shares a playlist with a friend. Only Lena is allowed to remove a song.
story.meaning: The application layer runs rules about what a user is allowed to do and what should happen as a result. The rule must run where the user cannot bypass it.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: Being able to send a request does not prove the friend owns the playlist.

steps.label: checks
steps.caption: The service checks the signed-in identity against the playlist's permitted editors.

steps.label: returns
steps.caption: The song stays in the playlist because the service rejected the change before writing it.

story.technology: A server-side API handler can authorize the caller and apply an allowed edit within a database transaction.

title: Microservices
lesson: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services organized around business capabilities. Each boundary adds network calls, versioning and failure modes, so it should buy real independence.
example: Separating video encoding from billing lets the encoding team scale GPU workers separately. A cross-service workflow now needs explicit handling of partial failure.
question: Which boundary provides the strongest case for a separate service?
answers: A video encoder with distinct scaling needs, data ownership and release cadence.
Two functions that always deploy together and share one transaction.
Two files that use different naming conventions.
why: Independent ownership and capacity requirements can justify the operational costs of a network boundary.
detail: Check how often a proposed boundary would force two teams to change and deploy together. A good service exposes a contract that can evolve while older clients continue working. It also controls its own data changes. Letting callers update its tables directly bypasses that contract and makes a later schema change risky for several teams.

terms.definition: Responsibility for deciding how a set of records is validated, changed and exposed.
The ability of existing clients to continue functioning after a service changes.

story.intro: An audiobook shop needs more workers to encode sound files, while its billing service is nearly idle.
story.meaning: Microservices split a product into services with distinct responsibilities that can be deployed separately. Each service owns the meaning and changes of its own data.

steps.label: uploads book to
steps.caption: The catalog records the new title and requests audio processing.

steps.label: adds
steps.caption: The team increases audio-processing capacity without deploying another copy of billing.

steps.label: reports completion to
steps.caption: Catalog marks the title playable only after it receives confirmation. It needs a way to recover if that message is delayed.

story.technology: A catalog API can publish an encoding job to a queue and accept a completion event carrying the book's ID.

title: Service Discovery
lesson: Service discovery turns a logical service name into current reachable endpoints. Instances register or are discovered as they start and stop. Clients or routing infrastructure must tolerate stale membership information.
example: A checkout service looks up inventory by service name while containers restart on new addresses. Health checks limit how long dead endpoints stay eligible.
question: New inventory containers receive fresh IPs on each rollout. How should checkout find them?
answers: Resolve a stable service name backed by an updated endpoint registry.
Build each container IP into the checkout binary.
Cache the very first container address indefinitely.
why: The registry decouples the calling service from short-lived addresses. Health and membership updates keep lookup results useful.
detail: A client can ask a registry for instances and choose one itself. Alternatively, it can send requests to a stable proxy that performs discovery and selection. The first approach puts discovery logic in each client. The second centralizes it in the proxy layer. Either approach needs a policy for expired registrations and failed connections.

terms.definition: A directory mapping logical service names to current endpoints.
A time-limited registration that an instance renews so stale entries eventually disappear.

story.intro: A checkout service needs the price of a mug. The pricing containers get fresh network addresses after every release.
story.meaning: Service discovery is how one service finds another when addresses can change. Checkout can keep asking for “pricing” even as the machines answering to that name come and go.

steps.label: registers with
steps.caption: The directory associates the pricing name with the instance's current address.

steps.label: looks up
steps.caption: Checkout uses the name from its configuration and gets an endpoint it can try.

steps.label: calls
steps.caption: The request reaches the replacement without changing checkout's code. A failed connection may require another lookup and retry.

story.technology: In Kubernetes, a Service provides a stable name and can route traffic to the ready pods selected for that service.
